title: We’ve been treating college as a career plan, but it’s failing too many students g-too-many-students
author: Patrick O’Donnell
source: The Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 24, 2026
summary: Patrick O'Donnell, a former CEO of a public charter school foundation, argues that the decades-long 'college for all' movement has turned the four-year degree into an expensive career exploration strategy with no exit ramp. He cites data showing that although most freshmen enroll to get a good job, more than half of graduates are underemployed a year out and 45 percent still are a decade later. Meanwhile the country faces an annual shortage of roughly 712,000 workers with certificates and associate degrees in well-paying fields. O'Donnell holds up Denver's Cherry Creek Innovation Campus, where students in an affluent suburb split their time between regular classes and hands-on career programs and leave with clarity about their paths. He acknowledges that bachelor's degrees pull ahead in return after about 15 years, but argues that shorter credentials can be the smarter first move for students who need economic traction. A student who spent two years in a nursing program before realizing it was not for her illustrates the cost of a system that never lets students test a path before enrolling.
points: Eighty-eight percent of freshmen enroll largely to get a good job, yet more than half of graduates are underemployed a year out and 45 percent a decade later.
Georgetown estimates an annual shortage of nearly 712,000 workers with certificates and associate degrees in jobs paying upward of $55,000.
Cherry Creek's program gives students real field experience so that those who do go to college enroll with direction and purpose.
Associate degrees and certificates often beat bachelor's degrees on return in the first decade, though the bachelor's pulls ahead after about 15 years.
O'Donnell argues 'college for all' created a false binary between academic preparedness and workforce skills.
quotes: For decades, Americans have been treating college as a career plan, spurred by the “college for all” movement—a decades-long educational and political push that aimed to make a four-year college degree the standard expectation and primary goal for all high school students. The data show that it doesn’t work.
These aren’t students who dropped out or gave up. They did everything right and still couldn’t find their footing.
The problem isn’t that college doesn’t matter. It’s that college has become an expensive career exploration strategy, with no exit ramp for students who may need one.

The common thread they shared was that they were all locked in on their career paths. They had real experience in the field from the Cherry Creek Innovation Campus and clarity that they were moving in the right direction.
That nuance matters: For students who need economic traction now, shorter-term credentials can be the smarter first move.
The “college for all” movement, while well-intentioned, has created a false binary between academic preparedness and workforce skills.

Two years gone—not because she failed, but because the system never gave her a chance to figure out her path before she enrolled. What’s worse, most students in this situation are left saddled with student loan debt.
